section.heading: 4.8 Applications to Difference Equations
section.paragraph: Continuing our study of discrete-time signals, in this section we explore difference equations, a valuable tool used to filter the data contained in signals. Even when a differential equation is used to model a continuous process, a numerical solution is often produced from a related difference equation. This section highlights some fundamental properties of linear difference equations that are explained using linear algebra.
section.heading: Linear Independence in the Space 𝕊 of Signals
section.paragraph: To simplify notation, we consider a set of only three signals in $$\mathbb{S}$$ , say, $$\{ u_{k}\}$$ , $$\{ v_{k}\}$$ , and $$\{ w_{k}\}$$ . They are linearly independent precisely when the equation
$$c_{1} u_{k} + c_{2} v_{k} + c_{3} w_{k} = 0 \text{for} \text{all} k$$

implies that $$c_{1} = c_{2} = c_{3} = 0$$ . The phrase “for all $$k$$ ” means for all integers—positive, negative, and zero. One could also consider signals that start with $$k = 0$$ , for example, in which case, “for all $$k$$ ” would mean for all integers $$k \geq 0$$ .
Suppose $$c_{1}$$ , $$c_{2}$$ , $$c_{3}$$ satisfy (1). Then equation (1) holds for any three consecutive values of $$k$$ , say, $$k,k + 1$$ , and $$k + 2$$ . Thus (1) implies that
and

$$\left[\right. u_{k} & v_{k} & w_{k} u_{k + 1} & v_{k + 1} & w_{k + 1} u_{k + 2} & v_{k + 2} & w_{k + 2} \left]\right. \left[\right. c_{1} c_{2} c_{3} \left]\right. = \left[\right. 0 0 0 \left]\right. \text{for} \text{all} k$$

The coefficient matrix in this system is called the Casorati matrix, $$C(k)$$ , of the signals, and the determinant of the matrix is called the Casoratian of $$\{ u_{k}\}$$ , $$\{ v_{k}\}$$ , and $$\{ w_{k}\}$$ . If the Casorati matrix is invertible for at least one value of $$k$$ , then (2) will imply that $$c_{1} = c_{2} = c_{3} = 0$$ , which will prove that the three signals are linearly independent.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Verify that $$\{ 1^{k}\}$$ , $$\{( - 2)^{k}\}$$ , and $$\{ 3^{k}\}$$ are linearly independent signals.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The Casorati matrix is

$$\left[\right. 1^{k} & \left(\left(\right. - 2 \left.\right)\right)^{k} & 3^{k} 1^{k + 1} & \left(\left(\right. - 2 \left.\right)\right)^{k + 1} & 3^{k + 1} 1^{k + 2} & \left(\left(\right. - 2 \left.\right)\right)^{k + 2} & 3^{k + 2} \left]\right.$$
Row operations can show fairly easily that this matrix is always invertible. However, it is faster to substitute a value for $$k$$ —say, $$k = 0$$ —and row reduce the numerical matrix:
$$\left[\right. 1 & 1 & 1 1 & - 2 & 3 1 & 4 & 9 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & 1 & 1 0 & - 3 & 2 0 & 3 & 8 \left]\right. sim \left[\right. 1 & 1 & 1 0 & - 3 & 2 0 & 0 & 10 \left]\right.$$
The Casorati matrix is invertible for $$k = 0$$ . So $$\{ 1^{k}\}$$ , $$\{( - 2)^{k}\}$$ , and $$\{ 3^{k}\}$$ are linearly independent.

section.paragraph: If a Casorati matrix is not invertible, the associated signals being tested may or may not be linearly dependent. (See Exercise 35.) However, it can be shown that if the signals are all solutions of the same homogeneous difference equation (described below), then either the Casorati matrix is invertible for all $$k$$ and the signals are linearly independent, or else the Casorati matrix is not invertible for all $$k$$ and the signals are linearly dependent. A nice proof using linear transformations is in the Study Guide.
section.heading: Linear Difference Equations
section.paragraph: Given scalars $$a_{0},\ldots \text{,} a_{n}$$ , with $$a_{0}$$ and $$a_{n}$$ nonzero, and given a signal $$\{ z_{k}\}$$ , the equation
$$a_{0} y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} = z_{k} \text{for all} k$$

is called a linear difference equation (or linear recurrence relation) of order $$n$$ . For simplicity, $$a_{0}$$ is often taken equal to 1. If $$\{ z_{k}\}$$ is the zero sequence, the equation is homogeneous; otherwise, the equation is nonhomogeneous.

In digital signal processing (DSP), a difference equation such as (3) describes a linear time invariant (LTI) filter, and $$a_{0},\ldots \text{,} a_{n}$$ are called the filter coefficients. The shift LTI transformations $$S(\{ y_{k}\}) = \{ y_{k - 1}\}$$ and $$S^{- 1}(\{ y_{k}\}) = \{ y_{k + 1}\}$$ were introduced in Example 1 of Section 4.7 and are used here to describe the LTI filter associated with a linear difference equation. section.paragraph: In many applications, a sequence $$\{ z_{k}\}$$ is specified for the right side of a difference equation (3), and a $$\{ y_{k}\}$$ that satisfies (3) is called a solution of the equation. The next example shows how to find solutions for a homogeneous equation.

We will not consider the case in which $$r$$ is a repeated root of the auxiliary equation. When the auxiliary equation has a complex root, the difference equation has solutions of the form $$\{ s^{k} \text{cos} k\omega\}$$ and $$\{ s^{k} \text{sin} k\omega\}$$ , for constants $$s$$ and $$\omega$$ . section.heading: Solution Sets of Linear Difference Equations
section.paragraph: Given $$a_{1},\ldots \text{,} a_{n}$$ , recall that the LTI transformation $$\left. T:\mathbb{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{S} \right.$$ given by
transforms a signal $$\{ y_{k}\}$$ into the signal $$\{ w_{k}\}$$ given by
$$w_{k} = y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} \text{for all} k$$
This implies that the solution set of the homogeneous equation
$$y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} = 0 \text{for all} k$$

is the kernel of $$T$$ and describes the signals that are filtered out or transformed into the zero signal. Since the kernel of any linear transformation with domain $$\mathbb{S}$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbb{S}$$ , so is the solution set of a homogeneous equation. Any linear combination of solutions is again a solution.
The next theorem, a simple but basic result, will lead to more information about the solution sets of difference equations.

note.title: Theorem 19
note.heading: Theorem 19
note.paragraph: If $$a_{n} \neq 0$$ and if $$\{ z_{k}\}$$ is given, the equation
$$y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} = z_{k} \text{for all} k$$
has a unique solution whenever $$y_{0},\ldots \text{,} y_{n - 1}$$ are specified.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: If $$y_{0},\ldots \text{,} y_{n - 1}$$ are specified, use (7) to define
$$y_{n} = z_{0} - \left[\right. a_{1} y_{n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{1} + a_{n} y_{0} \left]\right.$$
And now that $$y_{1},\ldots \text{,} y_{n}$$ are specified, use (7) to define $$y_{n + 1}$$ . In general, use the recurrence relation
$$y_{n + k} = z_{k} - \left[\right. a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n} y_{k} \left]\right.$$
to define $$y_{n + k}$$ for $$k \geq 0$$ . To define $$y_{k}$$ for $$k < 0$$ , use the recurrence relation
This produces a signal that satisfies (7). Conversely, any signal that satisfies (7) for all $$k$$ certainly satisfies (8) and (9), so the solution of (7) is unique.

note.title: Theorem 20
note.heading: Theorem 20
note.paragraph: The set $$H$$ of all solutions of the $$n \text{th-order}$$ homogeneous linear difference equation
$$y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} = 0 \text{for all} k$$

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: As was pointed out earlier, $$H$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{S}}$$ because $$H$$ is the kernel of a linear transformation. For $$\{ y_{k}\}$$ in $$H$$ , let $$F\{ y_{k}\}$$ be the vector in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ given by $$\left( y_{0} \text{,} y_{1},\ldots \text{,} y_{n - 1} \right)$$ . It is readily verified that $$\left. F:H\rightarrow\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n} \right.$$ is a linear transformation. Given any vector $$\left( y_{0} \text{,} y_{1},\ldots \text{,} y_{n - 1} \right)$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , Theorem 19 says that there is a unique signal $$\{ y_{k}\}$$ in $$H$$ such that $$F\left\{ y_{k} \right\} = \left( y_{0} \text{,} y_{1},\ldots \text{,} y_{n - 1} \right)$$ . This means that $$F$$ is a one-to-one linear transformation of $$H$$ onto $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ ; that is, $$F$$ is an isomorphism. Thus $$\text{dim} H = \text{dim} \mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n} = n$$ . (See Exercise 52 in Section 4.5.)

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find a basis for the set of all solutions to the difference equation
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Our work in linear algebra really pays off now! We know from Examples 1 and 3 that $$\{ 1^{k}\}$$ , $$\{( - 2)^{k}\}$$ , and $$\{ 3^{k}\}$$ are linearly independent solutions. In general, it can be difficult to verify directly that a set of signals spans the solution space. But that is no problem here because of two key theorems—Theorem 20, which shows that the solution space is exactly three-dimensional, and the Basis Theorem in Section 4.5, which says that a linearly independent set of $$n$$ vectors in an $$n \text{-dimensional}$$ space is automatically a basis. So $$\{ 1^{k}\}$$ , $$\{( - 2)^{k}\}$$ , and $$\{ 3^{k}\}$$ form a basis for the solution space.

section.paragraph: The standard way to describe the “general solution” of the difference equation (10) is to exhibit a basis for the subspace of all solutions. Such a basis is usually called a fundamental set of solutions of (10). In practice, if you can find $$n$$ linearly independent signals that satisfy (10), they will automatically span the $$n \text{-dimensional}$$ solution space, as explained in Example 4.
section.heading: Nonhomogeneous Equations
section.paragraph: The general solution of the nonhomogeneous difference equation
$$y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} = z_{k} \text{for all} k$$

can be written as one particular solution of (11) plus an arbitrary linear combination of a fundamental set of solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation (10). This fact is analogous to the result in Section 1.5 showing that the solution sets of $$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$$ and $$A\mathbf{x} = 0$$ are parallel. Both results have the same explanation: The mapping $$\left. \mathbf{x}\mapsto{A\mathbf{x}} \right.$$ is linear, and the mapping that transforms the signal $$\{ y_{k}\}$$ into the signal $$\{ z_{k}\}$$ in (11) is linear.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Verify that the signal $$\{ y_{k}\} = \{ k^{2}\}$$ satisfies the difference equation
$$y_{k + 2} - 4 y_{k + 1} + 3 y_{k} = - 4 k \text{for all} k$$
Then find a description of all solutions of this equation.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Substitute $$k^{2}$$ for $$y_{k}$$ on the left side of (12):

$$\left(\right. k + 2 \left.\right)^{2} - & 4 \left(\right. k + 1 \left.\right)^{2} + 3 k^{2} & = \left(\right. k^{2} + 4 k + 4 \left.\right) - 4 \left(\right. k^{2} + 2 k + 1 \left.\right) + 3 k^{2} & = - 4 k$$
So $$k^{2}$$ is indeed a solution of (12). The next step is to solve the homogeneous equation
$$y_{k + 2} - 4 y_{k + 1} + 3 y_{k} = 0 \text{for} \text{all} \textit{k}$$
The auxiliary equation is
$$r^{2} - 4 r + 3 = \left(\right. r - 1 \left.\right) \left(\right. r - 3 \left.\right) = 0$$

The roots are $$r = 1 \text{,} 3$$ . So two solutions of the homogeneous difference equation are $$\{ 1^{k}\}$$ and $$\{ 3^{k}\}$$ . They are obviously not multiples of each other, so they are linearly independent signals. By Theorem 20, the solution space is two-dimensional, so $$\{ 1^{k}\}$$ and $$\{ 3^{k}\}$$ form a basis for the set of solutions of equation (13). Translating that set by a particular solution of the nonhomogeneous equation (12), we obtain the general solution of (12):
$$\left{\right. k^{2} \left.\right} + c_{1} \left{\right. 1^{k} \left.\right} + c_{2} \left{\right. 3^{k} \left.\right} , \text{or} \left{\right. k^{2} + c_{1} + c_{2} 3^{k} \left.\right}$$
Figure 2 gives a geometric visualization of the two solution sets. Each point in the figure corresponds to one signal in $$\mathbb{S}$$ .

section.heading: Reduction to Systems of First-Order Equations
section.paragraph: A modern way to study a homogeneous $$n \text{th-order}$$ linear difference equation is to replace it by an equivalent system of first-order difference equations, written in the form
$$\mathbf{x}_{k + 1} = A \mathbf{x}_{k} \text{for} \text{all} k$$
where the vectors $$\mathbf{x}_{k}$$ are in $${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ and $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix.
A simple example of such a (vector-valued) difference equation was already studied in Section 1.10. Further examples will be covered in Sections 5.6 and 5.9.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Write the following difference equation as a first-order system:
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: For each $$k$$ , set
$$\mathbf{x}_{k} = \left[\right. y_{k} y_{k + 1} y_{k + 2} \left]\right.$$
The difference equation says that $$y_{k + 3} = - 6y_{k} + 5y_{k + 1} + 2y_{k + 2}$$ , so

$$\mathbf{x}_{k + 1} = \left[\right. y_{k + 1} y_{k + 2} y_{k + 3} \left]\right. = \left[\right. 0 & + & y_{k + 1} & + & 0 0 & + & 0 & + & y_{k + 2} - 6 y_{k} & + & 5 y_{k + 1} & + & 2 y_{k + 2} \left]\right. = \left[\right. 0 & 1 & 0 0 & 0 & 1 - 6 & 5 & 2 \left]\right. \left[\right. y_{k} y_{k + 1} y_{k + 2} \left]\right.$$
That is,
$$\mathbf{x}_{k + 1} = A \mathbf{x}_{k} \text{for} \text{all} \textit{k} , where A = \left[\right. 0 & 1 & 0 0 & 0 & 1 - 6 & 5 & 2 \left]\right.$$

section.paragraph: In general, the equation
$$y_{k + n} + a_{1} y_{k + n - 1} + \hdots + a_{n - 1} y_{k + 1} + a_{n} y_{k} = 0 \text{for} \text{all} k$$
can be rewritten as $$\mathbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\mathbf{x}_{k}$$ for all $$k$$ , where

$$\mathbf{x}_{k} = \left[\right. y_{k} y_{k + 1} \vdots y_{k + n - 1} \left]\right. , A = \left[\right. 0 & 1 & 0 & \ldots & 0 0 & 0 & 1 & & 0 \vdots & & & \ddots & \vdots 0 & 0 & 0 & & 1 - a_{n} & - a_{n - 1} & - a_{n - 2} & \hdots & - a_{1} \left]\right.$$
